A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PAPE and share the main Folktables evaluation. All text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v2 has no appendix; v4's Appendices A–D were included in the assessment.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments across 959 dataset-model cases, benchmark comparisons, performance-change analyses and a sample-size study.

after.justification: v4 retains the original census-data experiments and reports additional original evaluations on eight TableShift datasets in Appendix D.2.

M1.justification: The core density-ratio estimation, weighted calibration and performance-estimation pipeline is retained. Appendix C.2 adds an optional sample-based variance criterion for choosing between PAPE and IW. This is an auxiliary decision procedure, not a redesign of PAPE or an established change to the evaluated implementation.

E1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds eight TableShift datasets, including education and healthcare tasks such as ASSISTments, College Scorecard, Diabetes and Hospital Readmission. Despite acknowledged overlap with Folktables, these broaden represented domains and introduce ID/OoD scenarios whose shifts need not satisfy the covariate-shift assumption.

E2.justification: COT is newly evaluated for accuracy in Table 1 and Figure 2, but not for F1 or AUROC. Figure 3 adds RT-mod to the sample-size comparison. CBPE and the other principal comparators were already evaluated in v2.

E3.justification: The main temporal splits, 2,000-observation chunks and 959 evaluation cases are retained. MASTE/RMSSTE become NMAE/NRMSE without changing their formulas. The new TableShift experiment introduces designated training, validation and test partitions, concatenating ID and OoD validation/test portions because some OoD subsets are too small.

E4.justification: Appendix D.2 explicitly tests competitiveness under unspecified shift types that may violate PAPE's covariate-shift assumption, adding a substantial robustness question and evidence in Table 2. The earlier sample-size study is retained in Appendix D.1 with the same chunk sizes and stride, although its comparator coverage and plotted results change.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 newly specifies a sample-based approximation for comparing estimator variances, adding a statistical estimation procedure. Experimental uncertainty reporting otherwise retains the 500 resamples used for normalization and the paired Wilcoxon test. Appendix A explicitly states that confidence intervals were omitted; no increased run counts or newly reported intervals are established.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises many values under the retained reported protocol: PAPE's accuracy error pair changes from 0.99/1.31 to 0.97/1.28, while its leading aggregate ranking remains. New Table 2 reports PAPE NMAE values of 1.52, 0.83 and 0.67 for accuracy, AUROC and F1. Figure 3 also changes method-labeled curves, placing ATC rather than IW highest at small chunk sizes.

T1.justification: v2 already contains a calibration-error bound. v4 substantially extends it with approximate multicalibration definitions, transfer lemmas, the imperfect-weight bound in Theorem B.4 and the variance analysis in Appendix C. Theorem 3.2 also changes the stated calibration condition to calibration of c composed with f, while its proof controls original-f levelsets, leaving an assumption gap.

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the advertised scope from data-type-agnostic classification and any performance metric to binary tabular classification and confusion-matrix-derived metrics. The introduction newly claims full metric distributions supporting valid confidence intervals, whereas v2 presents estimation intervals as future work. Superiority over evaluated benchmarks remains a core claim.

C2.justification: The new Discussion explains PAPE through calibration repair and smoothing relative to CBPE and IW. Appendix C qualifies variance advantages, allowing situations favoring IW. Existing concept-shift and support limitations gain dimensionality and reference-data requirements; the unsupported-region explanation changes from zero weights to undefined density ratios.

D1.justification: v4 discloses default LGBM classifier/regressor choices, calibration-selection reasoning, detailed F1/AUROC recipes and baseline calibration choices. These mainly document previously reported experiments rather than establish implementation changes. Appendix A.1's recipes contain inconsistent confusion-matrix/F1 formulas. The explicit paper-code repository link supplied in v2 is absent from v4.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to ensemble disagreement, optimal transport, calibration under shift and multicalibration. PAPE is repositioned explicitly as an extension of newly cited CBPE research, rather than merely presenting CBPE as a simpler comparator. This changes the account of its intellectual foundations and contribution.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and method exposition are extensively rewritten. The algorithm-first presentation becomes definitions-and-theory-first; discussion, limitations and future work receive dedicated sections. The sample-size study moves to Appendix D.1, and authorship/header text also changes.

P2.justification: Both algorithm blocks disappear into prose. Figure 2 changes from large vertically stacked panels to a compact horizontal arrangement with expanded comparator curves. Figure 3 is restyled, gains a logarithmic vertical scale and moves to the appendix. Table 1 gains COT, Table 2 is added, and page formatting changes throughout.

improvement.justification: The new TableShift evaluation, clearer applicability boundaries and expanded explanations provide substantial benefits over v2. However, Appendix A.1 introduces inconsistent confusion-matrix/F1 formulas and gives TN/(TN+FP) as FPR; Theorem 3.2's proof also requires stronger calibration control than its statement supplies. These undermine reproducibility and theoretical assurance. The PDFs do not establish whether the metric-formula errors are documentation-only or affect reported results, so the benefits and harms do not support a reliable net quality judgment.
